description: A short sample lecture used by offline orchestrator tests. Chunks carry the slide on screen; qa_answers are the presenter's scripted Q&A answers.

slides.text: Introduction to distributed systems and the CAP theorem overview
Consistency, availability, and partition tolerance trade-offs in practice

chunks.text: Today we are going to talk about distributed systems and why they are hard.
The core idea is that nodes communicate over an unreliable network.
The CAP theorem says you can only pick two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
In practice partitions do happen, so you really choose between consistency and availability.
A strongly consistent system refuses writes when it cannot reach a quorum of replicas.
An available system keeps accepting writes and reconciles conflicts later on.
Eventual consistency means replicas converge once the network heals between them.
Vector clocks and version vectors help us detect concurrent updates across nodes.
Quorum reads and writes let us tune the balance between latency and consistency.
We will finish with a look at how real databases apply these ideas in production.

qa_answers: Good question. Partitions do happen on any real network, so during a partition the practical choice is between consistency and availability.
Eventual consistency means the replicas converge once the network heals, and version vectors help detect concurrent updates.
Quorum reads and writes let you tune latency against consistency by choosing how many replicas must respond.
Real databases like Cassandra and Spanner make different trade-offs here.
